ISOLATED STORMS SATURDAY⛈️a cold upper-level low will move directly across western Washington and Oregon on Saturday, bringing widespread showers, much cooler temperatures and scattered thunderstorms! In fact, the Storm Predicted Center highlighted parts of the region in a general thunderstorm risk Saturday - although the entire region does have an isolated thunderstorm risk.

Isolated storms are possible from western Washington through western Oregon, including Seattle, Portland, Salem, Eugene and Medford. The greatest potential in western Washington is south of Snohomish County, while southern Oregon’s risk extends from the coast inland to the Cascades.

Any stronger storm could produce lightning, brief heavy rain, gusty winds and small hail. The unusually cold air overhead and proximity to the low and favorable shear may also support a low-end risk of cold-air funnel clouds—especially across coastal southwestern Washington and northwestern Oregon. Most remain brief and harmless but on rare occasions rotation can reach the ground.

Storm placement will be scattered so not everyone will hear thunder, but if a storm approaches, move indoors⛈️

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
The wreckage beneath Oppenheimer’s foot once held the world’s first atomic bomb.

#TBT #ThrowBackThursday

On September 9, 1945, J. Robert Oppenheimer and General Leslie Groves returned to ground zero at the Trinity site in New Mexico. Oppenheimer rests one foot on the remains of the steel tower that supported the device.

Nearly two months earlier, on July 16, the first nuclear explosion had destroyed that tower. The Manhattan Project had demonstrated that its plutonium bomb worked.

By the time this photograph was taken, atomic bombs had been dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and Japan had surrendered.

Oppenheimer had directed the Los Alamos laboratory; Groves had commanded the project. Here, both stand beside the physical remains of the test that preceded those bombings.

Uranus appears to reverse course today, but like every planet, it isn't truly moving backward.

On September 10, Uranus begins its annual retrograde, seeming to drift westward against the background stars. The cause is pure geometry: Earth, on its faster inner orbit, is overtaking distant Uranus, shifting our line of sight the same way a passing car appears to slide backward. At magnitude 5.6, Uranus sits at the edge of naked-eye visibility in Taurus, near the Gemini border. Look for it in the predawn eastern sky with binoculars or a telescope 🔭🔵

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
🌀 PEAK SEASON AND NO HURRICANES! 🌀

Here we are at the statistical peak of hurricane season...and still, not a single hurricane has formed in the Atlantic this season. And I am TOTALLY cool with that!

As of today, 2026 ranks third for the latest first hurricane of the season, but by tomorrow morning, we'll blow right past the two years currently tied for the record.

Even better, the tropics are completely quiet right now, with nothing expected to develop over the next 7–10 days. If that continues, there's at least a chance we could make it all the way to the end of September without a hurricane.

Obviously, there's still plenty of hurricane season left, so we can't let our guard down just yet.

But after some of the seasons we've endured over the years, it's pretty refreshing to see one setting records for inactivity instead of intensity!

items.author: JeffBerardelli
items.text:
‼️ Dust Bowl, left in the Dust!
Climate contrarians love to cherry pick summer of 1936 in the US. But zoom out…
Summer 1936 was about 1.36°C or 2.45°F cooler 🥶 globally, than 2026.
Some context: US Summer 1936 was extreme in the plains Dust Bowl and adjacent areas. In fact, nearly half of U.S. states still have an all-time record high temp that was set during the Dust Bowl era.
The warming was localized to the US, but the warm bubble helped establish a high amplitude quasi stationary wave pattern in the Summer of 1936 (bottom map) across the northern hemisphere. If you look closely you can see the pattern of warm, cool, warm, cool, warm from the US-Atlantic - Europe. Some of the Dust Bowl was caused by poor human farming practices, and mowing down of native prairie grass, which shows you how humans can indeed impact the large scale climate. Impressive. But if you look closely enough at 1936 you can see a cold pool over the eastern Pacific, which helped establish the overall atmospheric wave pattern. Hand in hand, nature and humans worked to make the 1930s summers in the Plains intolerable. 
But zoom out and you’ll see human-caused global warming dwarfs the Dust Bowl. Modern climate change is global. Dust Bowl heat was mainly regional. 
Data: ERA & Berkeley Earth.

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
On September 10, 2008, the Large Hadron Collider fired up for the very first time, sending a beam of protons racing all the way around its 27-kilometre ring buried beneath the border of France and Switzerland.

It's the biggest and most complex machine humans have ever built, and that morning, after decades of planning and construction, engineers watched a single dot of light confirm the beam had made the full loop. The control room broke into applause.

The doomsday fears were never taken seriously by physicists. The collisions the LHC produces happen naturally when cosmic rays hit our atmosphere, and Earth has survived those for billions of years.

Just nine days later, an electrical fault caused serious damage and shut the collider down for over a year. But it recovered. And in 2012, the LHC delivered what it was built for: the discovery of the Higgs boson, the particle that gives mass to matter.

Today it's still running, still smashing particles together, still hunting for whatever lies beyond the physics we currently understand.

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🔥 Betelgeuse’s fiery, bubbling face has been seen in stunning detail.

Using ALMA, astronomers have imaged the inner atmosphere of Betelgeuse, the famous red supergiant in Orion that will one day explode as a supernova.

Betelgeuse is so huge that if it replaced the Sun, its outer layers would reach far beyond the orbit of Mars.

That enormous size lets telescopes resolve features across its atmosphere, something we cannot do for most stars.

The new ALMA observations show that Betelgeuse is not a smooth glowing sphere.

Its atmosphere is distorted, corrugated and marked by giant hot patches.

One of these regions is about 800 K hotter than the surrounding gas.

Even stranger, the brightest hot spot appears in almost the same location as it did in ALMA data from 2015.

That means some structures in Betelgeuse’s atmosphere may survive for at least seven years, much longer than current models of giant convection predict.

These hot patches are likely linked to huge rising cells of gas that drive shocks through the star’s outer layers.

That matters because this violent activity may help Betelgeuse shed material into space before its final explosion.

We are not just seeing a star.

We are watching a dying giant change before our eyes.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Dent et al., “ALMA high resolution observations of Betelgeuse: Persistent structure spanning the inner atmosphere”, Astronomy & Astrophysics (2026)

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
PEAK OF HURRICANE SEASON

Wind shear and dry air have slammed the door on tropical development! No tropical systems are expected to develop for at least 7 days. Gotta love it!

Today (September 10th) is the historical peak of hurricane season. It's the one day in 174 years of reliable records that you are most likely to have a tropical storm or hurricane in the Atlantic Ocean. While it's statistically all downhill from here, history tells us we can't let our guard down. We've had many huge hits from hurricanes after this date, including:

Cat. 1 Florence in 2018
Cat. 1 Matthew in 2016
Cat. 2 Floyd in 1999
Cat. 4 Hugo in 1989
Cat. 4 Hazel in 1954

The latest we've ever been hit was October 31st, 1899. That hurricane was a Category 2 that made landfall in Myrtle Beach. Bet that wasn't a good night for trick-or-treating!

This year is a little different because of El Niño. I’m certainly not saying we can’t get hit, but El Niño does tend to make it much harder for storms to develop and strengthen in our part of the Atlantic.

ISO. STORMS SATURDAY⛈️a cold upper-level low will move directly across western Washington and Oregon on Saturday, bringing widespread showers, much cooler temperatures and scattered thunderstorms. In fact, the Storm Predicted Center just highlighted parts of the region in a general thunderstorm risk Saturday - although the entire region does have an isolated thunderstorm risk.

Isolated storms are possible from western Washington through western Oregon, including Seattle, Portland, Salem, Eugene and Medford. The greatest potential in western Washington is south of Snohomish County, while southern Oregon’s risk extends from the coast inland to the Cascades.

Any stronger storm could produce lightning, brief heavy rain, gusty winds and small hail. The unusually cold air overhead and proximity to the low and favorable shear may also support a low-end risk of cold-air funnel clouds—especially across coastal southwestern Washington and northwestern Oregon. Most remain brief and harmless but on rare occasions rotation can reach the ground.

Storm placement will be scattered so not everyone will hear thunder, but if a storm approaches, move indoors⛈️

NORTHWEST WEEKEND STORM🌧️⛈️💨🏔️❄️a strong storm system will move from the Pacific Northwest coast into the interior late Friday into Saturday and Sunday, bringing a significant change to cooler, wetter and locally windy weather!

Friday will largely be a transition day. Western Washington and Oregon will largely remain mainly dry but noticeably cooler, while breezy post-frontal winds continue across parts of eastern Washington, eastern Oregon and Idaho. 

Rain will spread inland across western Washington and Oregon on Saturday. Most of northwestern Oregon and western Washington will receive around 0.15-0.50 inch, with locally higher amounts in the Coast Range and Cascades. Southern Oregon will receive around 0.15-0.25 inch near the coast and north of the Rogue-Umpqua Divide, with lighter amounts farther south into northwestern California.
A few thunderstorms are possible from western Washington through western Oregon, including a low-end possibility of cold-air funnel clouds. Temperatures could fall 5-20 degrees below normal.

The system will reach eastern Washington and Oregon later Saturday into Sunday. Widespread wetting rain is possible, with the greatest chances across the Cascades, Blue Mountains, southeast Washington and the southern to central Idaho Panhandle. A slower storm track would produce a narrow band of 1.25-1.75 inches across parts of southeastern Washington and the Idaho Panhandle. Embedded thunderstorms may create locally heavier downpours, ponding on roads, rising creeks and an increased risk of rockslides. Winds will gust 30-35 mph in parts of central and eastern Washington. Across western Idaho and southeast Oregon, the strongest front arrives late Saturday. Gusts of 40-50 mph are possible from the lower Snake River Plain southward toward the Nevada border. Showers and thunderstorms will favor the central Idaho mountains and parts of eastern Oregon, continuing into Sunday morning. Snow levels will fall to around 6,500 to 7,000 feet, allowing light snow to reach the higher mountain peaks. Heavier snow is likely across the mountains in Idaho into Montana and Wyoming.

Conditions will gradually dry from west to east Sunday, although showers may linger into the morning around the Cascades, eastern Washington and Idaho. The exact track and speed of the low remain important and could shift the corridor of heaviest precipitation🌧️⛈️💨🏔️❄️

ISS FLYOVER AT 8:30 PM

Despite some high clouds around, it should be a great evening to see the International Space Station fly overhead. Look up at 8:30 pm! If you've never seen it, the ISS looks like a bright point of light (as bright as Venus) moving steadily across the sky. It will appear in the southwest sky and then disappear in the northeast sky. In reality, the ISS is moving at over 17,500 mph and is 250 miles above us!

That brilliant “light” you see from the ground is not a headlight or other light on the ISS. You’re seeing sunlight reflected off the enormous station, particularly its solar arrays and other reflective surfaces. The solar arrays alone cover roughly half an acre.

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🚀 Europe just opened a new route to space.

German startup Isar Aerospace has successfully launched its Spectrum rocket from Andøya Spaceport in northern Norway.

The mission, called Onward and Upward, lifted off on September 5, 2026, at 10:12 p.m. CEST.

A little over seven minutes later, Spectrum reached orbit.

That makes Isar Aerospace the first European commercial space company to successfully deliver satellites into orbit using its own launch vehicle.

The achievement is especially important because the launch happened from continental Europe.

Europe has launched rockets before, mainly from French Guiana in South America. But launching to orbit from European soil has been a much harder milestone.

Spectrum is a two-stage rocket, about 28 meters tall, designed to carry up to 1,000 kilograms to low Earth orbit.

This was only its second flight.

Its first test launch in March 2025 lasted about 30 seconds before the rocket fell into the sea. But Isar treated that as part of the learning curve, fixed the problem, and returned with a successful orbital mission.

This time, Spectrum carried five CubeSats and one experiment.

For Europe’s private space industry, this was more than a launch.

It was proof that a new commercial path to orbit has begun.

📄 MISSION
📌 Isar Aerospace, “History for European spaceflight: Isar Aerospace reaches orbit and deploys payloads on second flight”, Onward and Upward Mission, 2026

items.author: NTXWC
items.text:
The afternoon high-res data is in. Here is an idea of what kind of rainfall we might be dealing with on Thursday. 

I've drawn a zone, mainly situated northwest of the metroplex, where some locations could see rainfall totals over an inch. I have about a 60% coverage of showers and storms Thursday pm close to the Red River, with coverage gradually decreasing towards the metroplex (10-20%)

Now, as you can see, many places in the red circle may see nothing at all. That's the nature of storms this time of year- without large systems swinging through, storms don't move all that much, and don't stay organized for very long, leaving to scattered instances of heavy rainfall. So while I can't say for sure who will see a storm, those in the red circle and along the Red River have the highest chance to see brief downpours capable of multi-inch rainfall totals, lightning, and gusty winds. 

As for the metroplex, it depends how much outflow is produced and how far southeast it pushes.

It's certainly the best chance for rain we've seen since early July, but it won't provide much relief for most.

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
A mysterious low-frequency hum has been detected by pulsar timing arrays, networks of rapidly spinning neutron stars used as cosmic clocks.

The leading explanation is that this hum comes from pairs of supermassive black holes slowly spiraling together across the Universe.

But a new study asks a deeper question.

Where did the ancestors of those enormous black holes come from?

One possibility is Dark Stars, a hypothetical first generation of stars powered not mainly by nuclear fusion, but by energy linked to dark matter.

In some models, these objects could grow huge, reaching up to a million times the mass of the Sun before collapsing into massive black holes.

Over billions of years, those early black hole seeds could grow, merge with others, and eventually form the supermassive black hole binaries that generate today’s gravitational-wave background.

The researchers found that if Dark Star remnants were common enough, their descendants could make a major, possibly dominant, contribution to the signal detected by pulsar timing arrays.

This does not prove Dark Stars existed.

But it gives scientists a new way to test the idea.

A faint cosmic hum today may carry the aftershock of stars that formed more than 13 billion years ago.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Ghodla et al., “Reconstructing PTA measurements via early seeding of supermassive black holes”, Physical Review D (2026)

3 MORE TROPICAL AREAS TO WATCH IN THE PACIFIC🌴🌀🌊behind Lowell, Marie and Karina, the Pacific remains very active with three separate areas now being monitored for possible tropical development.

The most immediate is EP96, located south-southwest of Baja California. Organization continues to improve, and a tropical depression is expected to form later today or tonight as it tracks west-northwest at 10-15 mph. Development odds have climbed to 90% through both 48 hours and 7 days.

Farther east, another area of low pressure is forecast to form several hundred miles south of Baja this weekend or early next week. Gradual development is possible as it also moves west-northwest, with a 40% chance of tropical development during the next 7 days.

A third area is particularly worth watching for Hawaii. A l ow pressure is forecast to form south-southeast of the islands, with gradual development possible late this week into the weekend as it moves slowly north-northwest. Development odds currently sit at 20% over the next 7 days.

There is NO imminent tropical threat to Hawaii or Southern California from any of these systems right now. However, Hawaii and Southern California will need to monitor the tropics closely over the next week. Even systems that remain well offshore can eventually send long-period swells toward the islands or the Southern California coast, producing larger surf, stronger rip currents and potentially additional coastal impacts depending on their eventual strength, size and track. Lots to watch across the Pacific as we move deeper into September🌴🌀🌊

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🌌 Newton’s 300-year-old law of gravity has just passed its biggest test yet.

For centuries, Newton’s inverse-square law has told us that gravity weakens with the square of distance.

It works beautifully in the Solar System. But scientists have long wondered whether gravity still behaves the same way across the largest structures in the Universe.

Now, astronomers have tested it using galaxy clusters separated by tens to hundreds of millions of light-years.

The team combined cosmic microwave background maps from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope with galaxy data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey.

As ancient light from the Big Bang passed through hot gas around moving galaxy clusters, it picked up tiny shifts called the kinematic Sunyaev-Zel’dovich effect.

Those shifts revealed how fast pairs of clusters are falling toward each other under gravity.

The result was striking.

Across scales of 30 to 230 megaparsecs, gravity weakened almost exactly as Newton predicted.

The study found the force followed roughly 1/r², with a measured value of n = 2.1 ± 0.3.

This does not solve the dark matter mystery.

But it does make one idea harder to defend: that gravity simply changes on enormous cosmic scales.

Newton’s law survived the largest test ever thrown at it.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Gallardo et al., “Test of the Gravitational Force Law on Cosmological Scales Using the Kinematic Sunyaev-Zel’dovich Effect”, Physical Review Letters (2026)

61 YEARS AGO — Hurricane #Betsy made landfall in SE #Louisiana near Grand Isle as a Category 4.  

Its track was one of the most unique you will ever see.  It looked like it would curve north away from the Gulf Coast twice, but high pressure built back in both times and forced it westward. 

My parents have told me many stories of this storm.  My dad told me the news said the worst was over and they could go to sleep.  Then he said he was woken up with water rising quickly into his room.  He lived in Arabi at the time. 

Levees breached and several areas including Gentilly, the Upper Ninth Ward, the Lower Ninth Ward as well as Arabi and Chalmette were flooded up to 8 feet of water in spots.  Nearly 164,000 homes were flooded, with about 60,000 people stranded in the city.  Many had to be rescued by boat and helicopter. 

For a generation, Betsy was “the storm” — the one parents and grandparents often referenced.  Betsy was a warning of how vulnerable New Orleans truly was, decades before Katrina would confirm that vulnerability once again.

One year from now, day will turn to night over the land of the pharaohs, for longer than any eclipse in a lifetime.

On August 2, 2027, a total solar eclipse sweeps across southern Spain, North Africa, and the Arabian Peninsula, and near Luxor, Egypt, totality will last up to 6 minutes and 23 seconds. That's extraordinary. Most total eclipses give just two or three minutes. This is the longest totality visible from easily accessible land until the year 2114, earning it the nickname "eclipse of the century."

The path of the Moon's shadow crosses Spain, Morocco, Algeria, Libya, Egypt, and Saudi Arabia. Luxor sits almost dead centre, where the eclipsed Sun will hang nearly overhead at about 82 degrees, and the region offers roughly an 80% chance of clear August skies, among the most reliable anywhere on the path.

⚠️ Certified eclipse glasses are essential except during totality itself. If you can travel to the path, start planning now 🌑☀️

🌌  For a few nights next week, two galaxies will grace the sky at once, and it may be your last good look at the Milky Way's heart this year.

The New Moon on September 11 brings the darkest skies of the month, with the ideal window running roughly September 8 to 14. With no moonlight to wash out faint light, this is one of the final chances in 2026 for Northern Hemisphere observers to see the glowing core of our own Milky Way before it slips below the horizon until spring.

Just after darkness falls, look low toward the southwest to find the Milky Way's central region in Sagittarius, marked by the Teapot asterism, its "steam" rising toward the galaxy's heart. It's a soft, mottled band of light, the combined glow of billions of stars 26,000 light-years away, threaded with dark dust lanes.

Then turn to the east. Climbing higher each hour, between the Great Square of Pegasus and the W of Cassiopeia, sits the Andromeda Galaxy (M31). At 2.5 million light-years, it's the most distant object visible to the naked eye, a faint oval smudge that becomes an elongated glow through binoculars. The light reaching your eyes left Andromeda before our species existed.

🔭 Get well away from city lights and let your eyes adapt for 20 to 30 minutes. No telescope needed.

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
When you lose someone you love, the quiet moments are often filled with memories. Late last night, during one of those moments, I came across one of the first selfies Mom and I took after she and Dad moved in with us 13 years ago.

She was so happy to be here, and we were just as happy to have them. We built our home with Mom’s needs in mind, making sure it was accessible and comfortable for her. I remember feeling like she and Dad had been given a new lease on life here and thinking how much they were going to enjoy it.

And they did.

In many ways, it was like they were on a permanent vacation. I took them along to so many of the events I was invited to, and before long, they became celebrities. It always made me smile when people recognized them, stopped to say hello or asked how they were doing. They loved it, and so did I.

So many wonderful memories were made over those 13 years. We’ll continue making them with Dad for as long as the good Lord allows, while always holding close the countless memories we were blessed to make with Mom.

It’s been more than six weeks since Mom passed, and I still think about her every single day. There are moments when the sadness hits, but more often now, the pictures and memories bring a smile before they bring a tear. I’m incredibly grateful for that.

I continue to receive heartfelt messages from so many of you sharing your own journeys with grief. Your stories have helped me tremendously, and I hope that by sharing mine, I’ve helped some of you too. As painful and lonely as losing someone can feel, there is great comfort in knowing that others understand, that others have walked this road, and that people genuinely care about your journey.

So, keep taking it one day at a time. There is no timetable for grief and no single “right” way to navigate it. The right way is whatever helps you keep moving forward while still honoring the person you love.

I’m learning that moving forward doesn’t mean leaving Mom behind. She comes with us in the stories we tell, the pictures that make us smile, the lessons she taught us, and all those little moments when a memory suddenly finds its way back.

And as long as those memories are with us, a part of her always will be too.

Miss you, Mom. Always will.
❤️❤️❤️❤️

🪐 Saturn has grown a giant 10-sided shape around its south pole.

NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope has revealed a huge atmospheric wave encircling Saturn’s southern polar region.

It is being called a decagon because it forms a strange 10-sided pattern in the planet’s clouds.

This is not a solid structure.

It is a wave trapped inside one of Saturn’s powerful jet streams, stretching through multiple layers of the atmosphere.

That makes it even more intriguing.

Saturn is already famous for its north-pole hexagon, a six-sided jet stream pattern that has been visible for more than 40 years.

But Cassini saw no sign of a similar long-lived structure in the south before its mission ended in 2017.

Hubble data now show that the southern decagon was already present by 2023, and it appears to be strengthening.

The pattern is also different from the northern hexagon.

It seems less stable, more mobile and still evolving.

Scientists do not yet know what created it, or how long it will last.

But Saturn has just become even stranger.

The planet with a hexagon now has a decagon too.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Sánchez-Lavega et al., “A decagon wave around Saturn’s south pole”, Science Advances (2026)

EAST TO WEST RADAR BLOOMS: Local radar sites across the eastern U.S. are lighting up with radar blooms. If you loop the radar, you'll note these blooms appear to be developing from east to west. These are birds being detected by radar, not actual precipitation (in most cases). But why are these blooms propagating westward? The answer? Nightfall. 

As Earth rotates from west to east, nightfall arrives on the east coast hours before the west coast. Birds wait to take off until after dark, aided by the relative protection night provides them. This means you'll see bird blooms on radar along the east coast first, gradually developing westward as sunset arrives and those westward birds then take off. This gives the appearance these radar artifacts are somehow traveling westward, when in fact, it's simply the byproduct of Earth's rotation and birds taking advantage!

🌡️ The world is now set to cross the 1.5°C global warming limit.

A new UNEP report says global temperature rise is likely to exceed 1.5°C within the next few years.

That does not mean one hot year has broken the Paris Agreement forever.

The 1.5°C limit is judged over long-term warming, not a single calendar year.

But the direction is now clear.

UNEP says even the most optimistic pathway sees warming peak around 1.8°C, while other scenarios go beyond 2°C.

Above 1.5°C, every extra fraction of a degree makes climate impacts more dangerous.

Heatwaves intensify. Wildfires grow. Floods become more destructive. Ecosystems weaken. Low-lying islands and coastal cities face rising risks.

The report says the best remaining path is now “overshoot, peak and decline.”

That means cutting emissions fast enough to keep the overshoot as low and short as possible, adapting to unavoidable damage, and eventually bringing temperatures back down.

Carbon removal will be needed, but it cannot replace deep emissions cuts.

This is not a permission slip to give up on 1.5°C.

It is a warning that the world must now fight to return to it.

📄 REPORT
📌 United Nations Environment Programme, “Limiting Overshoot: Navigating exceedance of 1.5°C and pathways towards return”, UNEP (2026)

items.author: GregDeeWeather
items.text:
HAWAII | Kauai Island Utility Cooperative update on post-Lowell recovery: 90% of customers without power. This is going to be a long, slow process as debris may be in the way of restoration. 

Full statement: 

"NEWS RELEASE: Hurricane Lowell caused significant damage to Kauaʻi Island Utility Cooperative’s transmission and distribution system as it passed over Kauaʻi overnight, leaving most of the island without power.

Approximately 90% of KIUC members experienced an outage at some point during the storm. As of this morning, approximately 33,000 of KIUC’s 36,000 member accounts remain without power.

KIUC crews began assessing damage this morning. With approximately 1,500 miles of transmission and distribution lines across Kauaʻi, the assessment and restoration effort will be extensive. Road closures, debris and other access limitations may also affect the ability of crews to reach damaged areas.

“Our first priority is making sure conditions are safe for our crews, emergency responders and the public,” said KIUC President and Chief Executive Officer David Bissell. “We know our members want to know when their power will be restored. Right now, we need to understand the extent of the damage and what repairs are necessary before we can provide reliable restoration estimates.”

Before damaged portions of the system can be re-energized, crews must inspect lines and equipment, identify damage and determine what repairs are necessary to safely restore power. As areas are assessed and conditions allow, repair and restoration work will proceed.
KIUC is mobilizing all available resources to restore power as safely and quickly as possible.

Given the extent of the storm damage, members should prepare for outages that may last several days or longer in some areas.

“This will be a significant island-wide restoration effort, and we ask for our members’ patience as our crews work to assess the system and begin repairs,” Bissell said. “We will provide restoration estimates as soon as we have enough information to do so responsibly.”

KIUC expects to provide another update this afternoon based on information gathered during the initial damage assessments.

Members are urged to stay well away from downed power lines and always assume that any downed line is energized. Downed lines and other electrical hazards should be reported to KIUC or emergency authorities.

Updates will be provided through KIUC’s website, social media channels and local news media as additional information becomes available."

items.author: maxvelocitywx
items.text:
The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season has the lowest accumulated cyclone energy to date...

While we have seen 5 named tropical storms this year, all of them have been weak and short-lived, with 0 storms reaching hurricane strength. This leads to why Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) matters: ACE is a metric used by meteorologists to measure the total wind energy output of a season by factoring in both the maximum intensity and the duration of every named storm.

Because ACE is calculated by taking the square of a storm's maximum sustained winds every six hours, weak tropical storms that quickly dissipate barely make a dent in the overall seasonal total. Through September 8, the 2026 season has generated an incredibly low ACE of just 4.40, undercutting the previous record low of 4.80 by this point in 1984.

For context on just how historically dormant the Atlantic basin has been, the long-term average ACE through this exact date is 45.91.

COOLER SOUTHERN WINTER | El Niño has been in the headlines for months for all its impacts. One that hasn't materialized yet is a cooler & wetter fall/winter for the southern U.S. 

The EURO monthly outlook shows this well. Though don't get too excited just yet. It's probably at least 6-8 weeks away. 

The maps below show how much above normal (red/orange) or below normal (blues) monthly temps will be across the U.S. 

September across the South looks pretty warm, with cooler-than-normal weather out west. We've definitely seen a lot of heat this month across the MidSouth & Lower Mississippi River Valley. 

The EURO shows that by Oct those "cooler-than-normal" conditions will begin to move east into the South-Central U.S. For the Southeast & Florida, temps in Oct. are still likely to be close to or just above normal. 

It's not until you get into Nov & Dec that the "cooler-than-normal" temps really start to take over the Southeast & Florida. This should also strengthen into January & February. 

The culprit? Rain! We'll see more rain events than normal, more fronts, more clouds & that should NUDGE temperatures lower. 

Just remember, we're talking about the AVERAGE over a whole month. Every day will NOT be cold. There will be normal days & there will be some warm or even hot days too. It's when you look at the month as a whole that you'll see the averages work out to be somewhat below normal.

Hang in there! Cooler weather is on the way.

items.text:
NW MOUNTAIN SNOW THIS WEEKEND🏔️❄️there’s an increasing signal for a cold early-season storm system to drop south out of Canada and into the Northwest and Northern U.S. Rockies this weekend into early next week.

The strongest signal currently exists across Idaho, Montana and Wyoming. Snow levels could fall to around 7,000 feet in parts of the region, potentially bringing the first meaningful accumulating snow of the season to some of the highest elevations. In fact, a foot or more could fall over the highest terrain, especially near Glacier National Park and along the Continental Divide.

The Sawtooths, Bitterroots, Glacier region, Tetons, Absarokas and Wind Rivers are among the areas worth watching. Some snow will also reach the highest peaks of Washington and Oregon, with possibly more depending on how cold and deep the system becomes. If you have plans to head into the high country this weekend, especially for hiking or fall colors, plan for winter weather conditions. Winter storm watches may be necessary for parts of Montana🏔️❄️

items.text: There’s a strong signal that the persistent heat dome will substantially weaken over the next week, allowing at least weak systems to dip into the Southern Plains! This will gradually increase moisture and rain chances across parts of Oklahoma, Texas and surrounding areas over the next week or two. Slightly cooler temperatures may also provide some relief from the persistent heat. Confidence in the specific details remains low this far out, but the overall pattern change is encouraging and the blend of models depicts this moisture potential along with the Climate Prediction Center beginning to highlight parts of the region in a zone to see above normal precipitation. Rain chances begin this week, favoring northern Oklahoma and southeast Texas🌧️⛈️📉
